If selection used the same folds that report its score, its metrics are optimistically biased. The selected feature set also differs across folds, which would be consistent with in-fold selection.

Ratios and interactions are computed on what look like categorical features (e.g. gill-color / cap-color). If these are ordinal-encoded, the arithmetic is arbitrary and encoding-dependent, so its semantics are unreviewed and the stability of these features is questionable.
Many engineered features were observed in only 1 of 3 folds with high importance (e.g. a mean normalized importance of about 0.20), so the importance estimates are unstable.
Decision-time and production availability of features is not documented. Odor and spore-print-color dominate importance, but their availability at the intended decision point is unreviewed.

The study used one model family with default hyperparameters (model_params is empty), and the dataset is known to be nearly deterministic in its features. The result may not generalise to other models or datasets.
Importance rankings are predictive and descriptive only and carry no causal meaning.
Duplicate rows and grouped or related samples were not assessed, which could inflate CV scores.
The bundle's limitations field is empty even though the claim lists a limitation.

challenges_to_claims.issue: The statement '1.0000±0.0000 ROC-AUC across folds' matches evidence.model_results[1].metrics.roc_auc, but it implies a stable, distinguishable lead. Competing models differ by only about 1e-5 to 1e-4 ROC-AUC, based on 3 folds and 1 repeat, and the zero std is not meaningful stability evidence.

The claim does not state that extra_trees ties the boosted models on accuracy, recall and F1, with the same fold-3 error profile, or that it has a recall miss at threshold 0.5 despite perfect AUC. Selecting on ROC-AUC alone hides this.

The claim's limitation covers the unseen holdout but omits unaudited duplicate rows, fold-size and sample-size uncertainty, and the absence of any decision-time or production-availability review of the raw features used.
'Algorithm family' ranking is based on default hyperparameters only. The lead of one family over others cannot be attributed to the family rather than to default settings.

decision: Retain extra_trees only as a provisional training-CV candidate, tied in practice with the boosted trees. Do not describe it as the strongest or a stable winner, do not claim generalization (the locked holdout is unseen), and do not approve for deployment or feature use. Next, run a repeated, duplicate-aware comparison before any holdout evaluation.

next_experiment.hypothesis: If extra_trees is genuinely better than the boosted trees, it will keep the best mean log loss and a lower or equal error count across repeated duplicate-grouped CV. If the lead is a ceiling artifact, paired differences will include zero and ranks will change between repeats.
next_experiment.success_gate: Pre-registered: run 5x repeated stratified 5-fold CV with identical splits for all four models, with rows grouped by identical feature vectors so duplicates never straddle folds. Report ROC-AUC, log loss and error count at threshold 0.5, plus the paired mean difference with a 95% interval versus the best competitor. extra_trees keeps its candidate status only if it is first on mean log loss in at least 80% of repeats and the paired log-loss interval versus the best competitor excludes zero. Otherwise record the models as statistically tied and choose by a pre-declared secondary criterion (error count, then runtime). Also list the specific fold-3 misclassified rows and their duplicate or label status. Decision-time availability review of odor, spore-print-color, gill-size and bruises is a prerequisite before any feature is endorsed.
next_experiment.title: Repeated, duplicate-grouped CV tie-break among extra_trees, xgboost, lightgbm and hist_gradient_boosting
next_experiment.why_smallest: It reuses the existing raw features and default models, adds only repeats and group-aware splits, and tests the single weak point, which is that the ROC-AUC ceiling and 3-fold design cannot separate the models. It involves no tuning, no new features and no holdout access.

risks_and_missing_evidence: Ceiling effect: ROC-AUC near 1.0 across models leaves the selection rule almost no discriminating power, so rank order may be determined by runtime or noise.
Only 3 folds and 1 repeat; the std of 0.0 is computed over 3 values and is not a reliable stability estimate.

The bundle gives no dataset row count, class balance, positive-class definition, or duplicate-row audit. Fold sizes implied by the metrics look small, but this is an inference and cannot be confirmed from the bundle. Duplicate or near-duplicate rows across folds could inflate CV scores, so group-aware splitting needs checking.

No decision-time or production-availability review of features such as odor, spore-print-color, gill-size and bruises. Some may be recorded only after consumption or lab inspection, or by an expert, so they may not exist at the real decision point. 22 features were used while the original dataset typically has 23; the bundle does not say which column was dropped or why.

Threshold fixed at 0.5 with no analysis of the asymmetric cost of false negatives versus false positives. Fold-3 recall of 0.996 for the top models suggests residual errors that matter if the positive class is the harmful one, but the bundle does not define the positive class.
All models are untuned baselines with empty model_params, so the comparison is between defaults and not between tuned algorithm families.
No preprocessing description (categorical encoding differs between linear and tree models), so effects of encoding on the comparison cannot be assessed. Pipeline fit inside folds is not documented.
Feature importances are model-specific, are not comparable across algorithms, and are empty for hist_gradient_boosting. They must not be read causally.
The empty limitations list in the bundle understates known caveats such as a single dataset profile and an unseen holdout.

challenges_to_claims.issue: The 'limitations' field is empty, though the evidence has several: unreported holdout size, no duplicate or leakage audit, and a degenerate bootstrap interval that conveys no real uncertainty. The claim also does not say which recipe was chosen. It names 'extra_trees/baseline', but no evidence path shows the selection outcome.
The claim does not answer the stated question about CV gain from optimization. No CV evidence is cited in the claim's evidence list.
Calling the 1.0000–1.0000 interval a '95% interval' can mislead. With a perfect score it only reflects resampling of an error-free sample.

The recommendation is reasonable, but its limitations list is empty. The cited importance and stability evidence is model-internal and says nothing about decision-time or production availability, and the evidence lists no per-feature availability review, so the stated criteria cannot yet be checked.
The importance method is unspecified, and 3-fold stability is thin. High importance for odor, gill-size, and spore-print-color must not be read as causal or as grounds for promotion.

decision: Accept EXP-035-C1 only as a narrow descriptive fact about this single holdout, and not as evidence of production readiness or of optimization benefit. Treat the optimization question as unanswered until the CV candidate scores are supplied. Keep EXP-035-C2 as a recommendation, with no features promoted. Do not reuse the consumed holdout for any further selection.

next_experiment.hypothesis: Optimization yields less than 0.001 mean CV ROC-AUC gain over baseline because of a ceiling effect, so baseline is correctly retained. Separately, the perfect holdout score is not driven by exact-duplicate overlap between training and holdout rows.
next_experiment.success_gate: Per-fold and mean CV ROC-AUC are reported for the baseline and every tuned candidate, and the gain is computed against the 0.001 threshold. The hypothesis is falsified if any tuned candidate improves mean CV ROC-AUC by 0.001 or more, or if the exact-duplicate overlap would alone account for the holdout's perfect score, meaning ROC-AUC stays at 1.0 only because duplicated rows are present. Also report holdout n and class counts, and the duplicate count with its share of the holdout. If there are duplicates, re-score a de-duplicated copy of the holdout using the existing frozen model, which is a descriptive check and not a new selection. For deployment-relevance, list for each top-10 stable feature whether it is available at the intended decision time and in production, using a documented review.
next_experiment.title: Report CV candidate scores and audit train/holdout duplicate overlap (no holdout reuse)
next_experiment.why_smallest: It uses only existing training CV outputs, an overlap check on data already split, and a documentation review. It requires no new holdout consumption, no new model families, and no new tuning.

risks_and_missing_evidence: No CV metrics, per-fold scores, candidate list, or tuned-versus-baseline delta are in the bundle, so the CV-gain question cannot be assessed (evidence.selection_rule is a rule only).
The holdout sample size, class balance, and split method are not reported. A perfect score on a small holdout is weakly informative.
Exact or near-duplicate rows between the training data and the holdout were not audited. Duplicates are common in categorical datasets like mushroom and could inflate the holdout score.
The bootstrap interval is degenerate under perfect separation and understates uncertainty. A bound such as a rule-of-three or exact binomial upper limit on error would be more honest.

A ceiling effect (ROC-AUC 1.0) leaves no room to detect differences between recipes. The 0.001 improvement threshold may be unreachable, which would make the 'baseline preferred' outcome uninformative.
The importance method (impurity-based versus permutation) is not stated. Impurity importance is biased toward high-cardinality categorical features and is unreliable under correlated features.
Stability rests on only 3 folds. The top-10 frequency is a coarse measure, and the ranking within the top 10 is not tested.

Features such as odor and spore-print-color may not be available at the real decision time, and the label definition may be entangled with them. No decision-time or production-availability review is documented, so no feature can be approved.
Calibration metrics are near zero, but with a perfect holdout they say little about calibration under distribution shift.
The dataset is a well-known benchmark, so this result may not transfer to any real deployment population.

challenges_to_claims.issue: '0 features triggered' is not backed by a trigger count or by complete profiles (10 of 57 shown), and the rule thresholds are missing. word_freq_3d (top_value_frequency 0.989375, null PSI) appears to deserve review but has empty production_risks.
Random-split PSI is acknowledged as a smoke check, yet the claim reads as a general absence of risk. Production-availability and temporal shift were not assessed.
The categorical-factorization limitation does not obviously match the float64 features shown, so the limitation text is not tied to this dataset's evidence.
The claim mixes the full-source row count (4601) with a training-only positive rate without stating train/holdout sizes or the holdout rate. The empty limitations list hides this.

decision: Do not proceed to modeling or approve any feature. Treat C1 as supported but incomplete. Treat C2 as unsupported until the full 57-feature profile, the rule thresholds and the null-PSI handling are shown. Decision-time and production-availability review has not been performed for any feature.

next_experiment.hypothesis: If the data-quality screen is sound, all 57 profiles will be reported, the null PSI on word_freq_3d will have a documented cause, any near-constant rule will be applied consistently, and no exact-duplicate rows will cross the train/holdout split. If any of these fail, claim C2 as written is falsified.
next_experiment.success_gate: All of the following are met: (1) 57 of 57 feature profiles are present, each with a non-null PSI or a documented reason for null; (2) numeric thresholds for the missingness, identifier, near-constant and PSI rules are recorded, and the count of triggered features is computed from the profiles and matches the claim; (3) word_freq_3d is either flagged under the near-constant rule or the threshold that exempts it is justified; (4) train size, holdout size, holdout positive rate and the split seed/method are reported; (5) the count of exact-duplicate rows is reported overall and across the train/holdout boundary. Fail if any item is missing, or if the triggered count differs from the claimed 0 without the claim being revised.

next_experiment.why_smallest: It requires no model training. A separate feature-by-feature decision-time availability review is still required before any feature is approved.

risks_and_missing_evidence: Only 10 of 57 feature profiles are in the evidence, so the claim of 0 triggered features cannot be audited.
No rule thresholds are given for missingness, identifier, near-constant or PSI review, so 'not triggered' cannot be interpreted.
word_freq_3d has a null PSI and a top-value frequency of 0.989375. It is unclear whether the null means constant, undefined, or skipped, or whether the near-constant rule failed to fire.
Split method, training size, holdout size and holdout positive rate are not reported. Inferred training size is about 3200 of 4601 rows.
No duplicate or near-duplicate row check is reported, including duplicates across train and holdout, which could inflate later holdout scores.

The label definition, feature derivation (how word frequencies are computed from raw emails) and data collection provenance are not in the evidence. Production availability of these derived features at decision time is unreviewed.
Only random-split PSI is reported. There is no temporal or source-based stability evidence, and the collection period is unknown.
The 'factorized categoricals' limitation appears unrelated to the observed float64 features, which suggests a generic limitation was copied into the package.
The empty limitations on C1 omit that the positive rate covers training data only.

The package gives no per-feature view of the positive rate or of feature-label association, so a leakage-like proxy cannot be ruled out. Predictive or association results would not establish causality in any case.

challenges_to_claims.issue: The claim is factually supported (detector_canary_passed = true) but has no listed limitations. It is easy to over-read as a clean audit; it only establishes detector sanity on an exact-target canary, not coverage of real columns or partial proxies.

The statement 'Declared decision-time exclusions: none' is cited to safe_vs_unsafe_training_cv, which is null, so the cited evidence does not support any conclusion. The empty list is a declaration, not evidence of absence of leakage. The claim is typed as a decision, but no decision-time semantics review is recorded to justify declaring no exclusions. It must not be read as approval of all features.

decision: Do not treat spambase features as cleared. Mark the leakage audit as incomplete: the canary check passes, but the column-level audit and the safe-vs-unsafe comparison have no recorded evidence. No feature is approved, because there is no decision-time or production-availability review on record.

next_experiment.hypothesis: If no spambase column is a target proxy or violates the prediction-time contract, then the detector will flag no column beyond review thresholds, and removing any flagged-for-review columns will change grouped-CV performance by no more than fold-to-fold variation. This is a predictive hypothesis only and says nothing about causal effects.
next_experiment.success_gate: Pre-registered before running: (1) the detector emits per-column records (name flag, univariate AUC, uniqueness) for all columns, with the AUC review threshold stated in advance; (2) the data owner records for every flagged column a decision-time and production-availability verdict; (3) safe_vs_unsafe_training_cv is populated, with duplicates grouped so they do not span folds and the metric reported as mean and std across folds; (4) the gate passes only if the safe-set metric differs from the full-set metric by less than the fold std, with no unreviewed flagged column. Any flagged column lacking a semantic verdict, or a non-null gap above the fold std, keeps the audit open.
next_experiment.title: Per-column leakage screen plus decision-time review and duplicate-aware safe-vs-unsafe CV on spambase
next_experiment.why_smallest: It reuses the existing detector and CV harness, adds only per-column output, a review record, and duplicate grouping, and fills the one null field that blocks any conclusion, without new models or features.

risks_and_missing_evidence: No per-column detector results are recorded (name-based flags, univariate AUC, uniqueness/near-uniqueness), so it is unknown which columns, if any, were flagged for review.
safe_vs_unsafe_training_cv is null: the performance impact of dropping suspect features was never measured, and it is unclear whether the comparison was skipped or failed.
Empty declared_leakage_features is ambiguous: it could mean a review was done and found nothing, or that no review was done. No reviewer, date, or semantics source is recorded.

No decision-time/production-availability review of the spambase columns is documented. Spambase features are aggregate word and character frequencies and capital-run-length statistics computed over the whole message; whether the same features can be computed at the intended prediction time (for example, before or after any downstream labeling or filtering step) needs to be stated by the data owner.

Known dataset-level concerns are unaddressed: possible duplicate or near-duplicate rows, and corpus-specific artifacts (for example, words or tokens tied to the original data source) that may act as proxies without being leakage in a production sense. Duplicates across CV folds would also inflate any validation score.
The canary tests only an exact-target copy. Detector sensitivity to partial proxies (noisy or transformed target encodings, features derived from labels or from post-outcome processes) is untested.
Because the detector's rules only propose review and cannot confirm leakage, a clean detector result would not be proof of no leakage even if per-column output existed.
The bundle's empty top-level limitations conflicts with the limitation stated in C2, so the record understates known caveats.

challenges_to_claims.issue: The claim cites training-CV only, but the study question asks about validation evidence. Nothing in the bundle shows a holdout or repeated-CV confirmation, and the stage was selected on the same CV that reports the score.

The claim omits that ratios scored higher on ROC-AUC (0.98799 vs 0.98694) and on the secondary metrics. Raw wins only through the 0.002 ROC-AUC tolerance and a parsimony preference, so the wording could overstate how well raw is supported.

Stated limitations cover only generic-feature semantics. They do not cover fold-internal fitting verification, duplicate rows, dataset-specific tokens (hp, george, edu), or production-availability review. The empty evidence.limitations list is inadequate.

'Use raw' is a recommendation for a screen, not a finding that engineered features lack value. The data cannot separate 'no effect' from 'too little power' with 3 folds and 1 repeat. The sharp drop of the selected stage also shows the feature-selection step has an unexplained failure.

decision: Retain raw as the baseline for the next model screen only, and keep ratios as a challenger. Do not treat this as feature approval or deployment readiness. Do not adopt the selected-stage feature set. Do not claim any engineered recipe improves performance.

next_experiment.hypothesis: Hypothesis: the ratios recipe gives a real ROC-AUC gain of at least 0.002 over raw once fold noise is reduced and duplicate rows are grouped. If the gain is smaller, the 0.00105 difference seen in EXP-038 is noise or a small effect below the practical threshold.
next_experiment.success_gate: On a fixed 5x3 repeated stratified CV with duplicate rows grouped (train split only), with ratio features fit inside each training fold, ratios must (a) exceed raw by at least 0.002 mean paired ROC-AUC difference, (b) have a paired bootstrap 95% CI lower bound above 0, and (c) not worsen mean log loss or ECE. Then confirm on an untouched holdout. If any condition fails, keep raw as the screening baseline. Passing the gate would not approve the ratio features. Separate decision-time and production-availability review would still be required.
next_experiment.title: Paired repeated-CV, duplicate-aware comparison of raw vs ratios
next_experiment.why_smallest: It compares only the two contenders, the best stage and the parsimonious stage, with the same model and params. It changes only the repeat count and the grouping or holdout protocol, so it directly tests whether the existing 0.00105 gap is real and checks the leakage and duplicate risk.

risks_and_missing_evidence: Only training-CV evidence is reported (3 folds, 1 repeat). There is no untouched holdout or temporal split, so 'validation evidence' is not established, and choosing a stage on the same CV used to report it is optimistically biased.

The evidence does not document whether the ratio, interaction and selection steps were fit inside each training fold. Feature selection and the interaction candidate list must be fold-internal; the varying observed_folds counts suggest per-fold selection but do not prove it.

Duplicate or near-duplicate rows and grouping are not reported. Spambase is widely reported to contain duplicate rows, which I have not verified in this package. If true, they could inflate CV scores and blur small differences between stages.

Features like word_freq_hp, word_freq_george and word_freq_edu look collection-specific (likely tied to the original mailbox). No decision-time or production-availability review was done for any feature, so none is approved. How each capital_run_length_* feature is computed and whether it is available at decision time are also unreviewed.

The 0.002 tolerance in the selection rule is not justified, and the rule ignores log loss, ECE, Brier and average precision, where ratios was at least slightly better than raw. No uncertainty is attached to the stage differences, and the 3-fold CIs overlap heavily.
Only one model (lightgbm with default params), one fixed threshold of 0.5, and no class balance or stratification details are reported. Conclusions may not transfer to other model families.
Importance values are not causal and are unstable for interaction features (observed_folds=1), so they should not be used to justify feature meaning.
The cause of the selected-stage collapse (25 features, ROC-AUC about 0.949) is not diagnosed. It may be a selector or protocol artifact rather than a property of the features.

challenges_to_claims.issue: The claim names hist_gradient_boosting as the candidate on the strength of a mean ROC-AUC lead of roughly 0.0004 to 0.0006 over lightgbm and xgboost. That lead is within fold std on 3 folds and 1 repeat. The wording is acceptably hedged ('training-CV model candidate'), but it omits that the top three boosters are effectively tied.
The '±0.0021' is fold std from only 3 values and is not an uncertainty interval for the mean. It could be misread as stability evidence.

The 'raw features' claim and the question's 'dataset profile' framing are not supported by any profile, duplicate check or leakage audit in the bundle. Feature availability at decision time is unreviewed.
Because models are compared only at default parameters, 'algorithm family' conclusions are limited to default configurations.

decision: Keep hist_gradient_boosting as a provisional training-CV candidate. Treat it as statistically indistinguishable from lightgbm and xgboost until a repeated paired comparison says otherwise. Do not call it the winner, do not touch or report holdout results, and do not approve deployment or any feature.

next_experiment.hypothesis: Hypothesis, not a finding: hist_gradient_boosting's ROC-AUC lead over lightgbm and xgboost at default parameters is real. It will persist under repeated, identically paired stratified CV, with a paired mean difference above 0 and a 95% interval excluding 0.
next_experiment.success_gate: Run hist_gradient_boosting, lightgbm and xgboost with the same seeds and identical folds, using 5 repeats of 5-fold stratified CV (25 paired evaluations) on the training split only. Do an exact-duplicate check and keep duplicates within a single fold. The hypothesis is supported only if hist_gradient_boosting has the highest selection score (mean − 0.25×std over all folds) AND the paired ROC-AUC difference against each competitor has a 95% interval excluding 0 (for example a paired bootstrap or corrected resampled t-test). Otherwise record the three as a statistical tie and break the tie on pre-declared secondary criteria (log loss, ECE-10, runtime). Do not touch the locked holdout.
next_experiment.title: Repeated paired stratified CV of the top three boosters (training data only)
next_experiment.why_smallest: It changes only the resampling design (repeats, pairing, duplicate handling) for the three contenders. It adds no new features, tuning, or holdout access, and directly tests whether the observed ranking exceeds split noise.

risks_and_missing_evidence: Only 3 folds and 1 repeat: the fold std (and so the 0.25×std penalty) is poorly estimated. The ranking among the three boosting models could flip under different splits.
Fold construction is not documented: stratification, seed, and whether the folds are paired and identical across models.
No duplicate or near-duplicate row check is reported. Duplicates across folds would inflate CV scores and could favor high-capacity models.
No dataset profile is included (class balance, row count, missingness), so the dataset-profile framing in the question cannot be verified.

All models run at default hyperparameters, so the ranking reflects defaults and not tuned capability. The selection rule also ignores accuracy, F1, log loss and calibration, where the differences among boosters may be as small as the ROC-AUC gaps.

The decision threshold is fixed at 0.5 and was not optimized or justified for any operating point. ROC-AUC does not guarantee good operating-point behavior or calibration (ECE-10 is about 0.025 to 0.057 across models).

Feature importances are missing for hist_gradient_boosting and are not comparable across models. Importance is not causal evidence. Dataset-specific tokens such as word_freq_george and word_freq_hp rank highly for some models and may reflect corpus artifacts. No decision-time or production-availability review has been done for any feature.
The runtime tie-breaker is not comparable: elapsed_seconds covers a single run on one machine, and hist_gradient_boosting is slower than lightgbm and xgboost in elapsed_seconds.
The locked holdout has not been used. This is correct for selection but means no generalization estimate exists.
The limitations list is empty at bundle level, even though the claim itself lists limitations.

challenges_to_claims.issue: The claim is labeled fact and its numbers match holdout_metrics and the bootstrap interval. However, 'preselected' and 'baseline' are not backed by any evidence field: no CV results, selected-candidate record or preselection log. The empty limitations list also omits that the interval covers test sampling only and that no duplicate-overlap check was reported.
The package question asks about CV gain from optimization, but the cited evidence contains only holdout metrics, so the claim does not address that question.

The recommendation cites top_final_features and cv_feature_stability, which are both empty, so no feature-level evidence supports or illustrates it. It is a sound policy statement but is not empirically grounded in this experiment, and no feature has been reviewed for decision-time or production availability.

decision: Do not conclude that optimization yields (or fails to yield) a meaningful CV gain. Treat C1 as a descriptive holdout result for one recipe only, pending the missing CV evidence. Do not promote any feature or approve deployment.

next_experiment.hypothesis: The best tuned candidate does not beat the baseline hist_gradient_boosting recipe by at least 0.001 mean ROC-AUC under paired repeated stratified CV (the null expectation implied by the baseline selection). Separately, exact-duplicate overlap between training and holdout rows is negligible.
next_experiment.success_gate: Report per-fold paired ROC-AUC deltas (tuned minus baseline) over at least 5x5 repeated CV with identical splits. The hypothesis is falsified if the mean delta is at least 0.001 and its 95% interval excludes 0. Report the exact-duplicate count between train and holdout. If it is above 0, flag the holdout score as potentially inflated and re-score on the de-duplicated holdout subset without re-tuning. Do not use the holdout for any selection.
next_experiment.title: Paired repeated-CV test of tuned vs baseline on training data only, plus train/holdout duplicate audit
next_experiment.why_smallest: It touches only training data and a row-hash comparison, needs no new models beyond the existing candidates, and directly supplies the missing CV-gain evidence and the main unchecked leakage risk.

risks_and_missing_evidence: No CV metrics, per-candidate scores, per-fold values or paired deltas, so the 0.001 gate cannot be verified (evidence.selection_rule is the only CV-related field).
No evidence that the recipe was preselected before the holdout was seen, such as a timestamped or logged choice. holdout_consumed=true shows consumption but not the order of choices.
Holdout size, class prevalence, split method and seed are not reported, so the precision of the interval and the metrics cannot be assessed.
No duplicate or near-duplicate audit between train and holdout. Spambase is known to contain repeated rows, so overlap could inflate the holdout score. This was not checked here.
The bootstrap resamples only the holdout predictions. It ignores training and seed variance, and 400 draws is modest for tail percentiles.
A fixed threshold of 0.5 was used with no threshold-selection or cost analysis. Precision, recall and ECE are tied to that threshold and to unknown prevalence.
Feature evidence is empty, so decision-time availability, production availability, stability and monitoring were never reviewed for any feature.
The limitations list is empty despite the gaps above.
Single dataset and single holdout, so no generalization claim is possible. The scores are predictive only and carry no causal meaning.

challenges_to_claims.issue: Asserts 0 features triggered review rules, yet only 10 of 17 features appear in evidence.feature_profiles. The conclusion is not supported for the remaining 7, which are likely the factorized categoricals.
Framed as a 'risk' claim but reads as reassurance. A zero-trigger result from rules that cannot assess decision-time availability or leakage should not be read as production readiness.

States 12330 rows and a 'training' positive rate with no limitations. The implied profile denominator (~3200 rows) and the unreported split sizes leave the relationship between source rows and training data unexplained.

Random-split PSI values (all below about 0.021) are being used as shift evidence. Random splits are expected to show near-zero PSI by construction, so they cannot show temporal or production drift, as the limitation already concedes.

decision: Hold modeling. Do not treat the dataset as cleared. Claim C2 is unsupported as written until all 17 features are profiled, the row denominators are explained, and each feature has a documented decision-time and production-availability review. No feature is approved.

next_experiment.hypothesis: If the profiling is re-run on all 17 features with raw categorical labels restored and explicit train/holdout row counts, then every feature will have a documented profile and an availability status, and at least one session-aggregated feature (e.g., PageValues, BounceRates, ExitRates) will be classified as requiring a prediction-time computation-window clarification. This is falsified if all 17 features are shown to be available at the intended decision point with documented timing.
next_experiment.success_gate: All of the following hold: (1) 17 of 17 features carry a profile (dtype, missing_rate, unique_ratio, top_value_frequency, PSI), with categoricals profiled on raw labels; (2) the train and holdout row counts and the sampling rule are reported and reconcile with the 12330 source rows; (3) the holdout positive rate is reported alongside the train rate; (4) every feature has a recorded status of available, unavailable, or unknown at the intended decision point, with its computation window cited, and no feature is approved while its status is unknown; (5) an exact-duplicate-row count across train and holdout is reported.
next_experiment.title: Complete 17-feature profile with row accounting and a decision-time availability table
next_experiment.why_smallest: It requires no model fitting. It only closes the coverage and denominator gaps in the existing profiling step and adds a documentation table, which is the minimum needed before the C2 claim can be accepted or rejected.

risks_and_missing_evidence: Profile coverage gap: 10 of 17 features are profiled, so the 'no review rules triggered' conclusion cannot be verified for the other 7 (EXP-041 / evidence.feature_profiles vs evidence.feature_count).

Row-denominator ambiguity: unique_ratio and the positive rate imply about 3200 rows, while source_rows is 12330. The train/holdout sizes, the sampling method, and the holdout positive rate are not reported.

Categorical semantics lost: factorized categoricals produce arbitrary integer codes. Numeric-looking profiles (PSI, unique_ratio, dtype int64) are not meaningful for them, and production encoders would need the raw categories (EXP-041 / claims[EXP-041-C2].limitations).

Decision-time and availability review missing: PageValues, BounceRates, and ExitRates are session-aggregated analytics metrics that may encode post-outcome or end-of-session information. Their computation window and timing relative to the prediction point are undocumented. The same question applies to the page-count and duration features, which may be final session totals.

decision: Provisional only: keep raw as the default baseline for the next screen, but not as a validated winner over feature engineering. Do not treat the recipe or any feature as approved. next_experiment.hypothesis: Adding ratio_ProductRelated_Duration_div_ProductRelated to the 16 raw features gives a paired mean ROC-AUC gain of at least 0.002 over raw. It is not shown that all transforms, ratio and interaction generation, and feature selection were fit inside each training fold. The 'selected' stage varies per fold, which suggests inner selection, but the evidence does not confirm leakage-free nesting.

Decision-time availability is unreviewed. Session aggregates (durations, ExitRates, BounceRates, page counts) may only be known at or after session end. Confirm that the prediction point matches their availability.

challenges_to_claims.issue: The claim names extra_trees the leader on a rule-score margin of about 0.0015 over logistic_regression, which has the higher raw mean ROC-AUC (0.7376 vs 0.7366). The fold scores and CIs overlap, and logistic_regression wins 2 of 3 folds. The lead comes from a noisy 3-fold std penalty, so it is not distinguishable from a tie.

The '±0.0072' in the statement is not labeled as a std (it matches the 3-fold sample std). Presenting it as a stability margin overstates precision at n=3, and the declared limitations omit the small fold count and 1 repeat.
The question asks about the 'algorithm family', but only default-parameter, untuned, single-run models were compared. The result cannot be read as a family-level ranking.

The claim does not address validation leakage (grouping, duplicates, time) or decision-time feature availability. Session-aggregate features such as ExitRates, BounceRates and the duration and page-count features have not been reviewed for production availability.
logistic_regression is better on log_loss, Brier and ECE and is faster. Choosing extra_trees on ROC-AUC alone ignores that probability-quality evidence and the runtime tiebreak.

decision: Retain extra_trees only as a provisional training-CV candidate, tied with logistic_regression. Do not describe it as the strongest or most stable family, and do not approve it for deployment or holdout promotion until the paired repeated-CV comparison below is complete. No feature is approved.

next_experiment.hypothesis: If extra_trees is genuinely better than logistic_regression on this dataset, its ROC-AUC advantage will be positive and its paired-difference CI will exclude zero under repeated CV on identical folds. Otherwise the 0.0015 rule-score lead is noise. This is a predictive-performance test only and says nothing about causes.
next_experiment.success_gate: Pre-registered, training split only. (1) Run both models on identical folds with 5 repeats of 5-fold stratified CV, and also with group-aware folds if a session or user key exists. (2) Deduplicate exact duplicate rows before splitting, or report scores with and without duplicates. (3) extra_trees is retained as leader only if the paired mean ROC-AUC difference (extra_trees minus logistic_regression) is at least +0.005 and its 95% CI lower bound is above 0. next_experiment.why_smallest: It reuses the two top candidates and the existing metrics, changes only the repeat count and the split-integrity checks, and tests directly whether the observed lead survives noise. It needs no new features, tuning or holdout access.

risks_and_missing_evidence: Only 3 folds with 1 repeat: the std and the 0.25×std penalty are unreliable, and a 0.0015 rule-score margin is well inside fold noise.

The CV split is not described. Stratification, grouping by user or session, and time ordering are all unspecified. online_shoppers sessions can share returning visitors, may contain duplicate rows, and cover a limited set of months, so random folds could inflate scores or distort the ranking. Month is a feature, which adds a seasonality risk.

No decision-time or production-availability review of the features. ExitRates, BounceRates, the page-count and duration aggregates (Administrative, Informational, ProductRelated and their durations) and SpecialDay may be computed over the whole session, including behavior after the decision point. Their availability when a prediction would be made is unverified.

It is not documented why the 16-feature raw set was chosen, or whether any columns (e.g. PageValues) were dropped for leakage reasons. The claim says 'raw features' without a preprocessing or encoding description, and the tree and linear models may be treated differently (scaling, categorical encoding, imputation).
All models use default hyperparameters, so the family comparison mixes algorithm differences with untuned-default effects.

The selection rule uses ROC-AUC only, with an arbitrary 0.25 std penalty. The runtime tiebreak is not applied and would favor the faster logistic_regression. The secondary metrics (log_loss, Brier, ECE) favor logistic_regression.

Threshold-dependent metrics at 0.5 (recall, F1) are close to degenerate for the minority class. The class prevalence and any cost context are not in the evidence, so these metrics should not support any operating-point claim.

Feature-importance stability is not comparable across models (logistic_regression importance is presumably coefficient-scale-based, trees are impurity-based). hist_gradient_boosting has none. Top-10 frequencies from 3 folds carry little weight, and importance is not evidence of causal effect.
The locked holdout has not been used. This is correct for selection, but it means the result is a training-CV estimate only.

challenges_to_claims.issue: The claim is factually supported as a point estimate and interval, but with empty limitations it omits the missing baseline comparison, the split design, the holdout size, and the bootstrap's failure to capture selection variance. It does not address the question's CV-gain half, and the recipe name is not verifiable from the evidence payload.
Any reading of the holdout score as evidence that optimization helped would be unsupported, because no baseline or tuned CV scores are included.

The recommendation is sound as policy, but the cited evidence shows only importance and fold frequency, not decision-time or production-availability review. Fold stability over 3 folds is weak, and importance cannot support causal or promotion claims. No feature should be treated as approved on this basis.

decision: Report EXP-045-C1 only as a descriptive holdout ROC-AUC with its interval. Do not claim that optimization produced a meaningful CV gain until paired CV evidence is provided. next_experiment.hypothesis: Hypothesis, not a finding: extra_trees_C02 improves mean ROC-AUC over the baseline by at least 0.001 under repeated stratified CV, with the paired fold-wise difference distinguishable from zero.

Session-level features such as ExitRates, BounceRates, and the duration and page-count features may be computed over the full session. Whether they are available at the intended decision time is unreviewed, and their top importance rankings do not settle that.

The importance method (impurity-based, permutation, or other) is not stated. Impurity importance in tree ensembles is biased toward continuous and high-cardinality features and is not a measure of causal or predictive necessity.

The feature list does not include PageValues, which is often present in this dataset. It is unclear whether it was deliberately excluded for leakage or availability reasons, and the exclusion is undocumented.
Calibration (ECE 0.0307) is a single holdout estimate with no interval, and the operating threshold for any downstream decision is unselected.
All limitation fields are empty, which understates the issues above.

challenges_to_claims.issue: The recommendation to 'use the ratios feature recipe' rests on a 0.0031 mean ROC-AUC gain over raw. The gain comes from one of three folds, ratios is lower in the other two, and the ci95 intervals overlap (raw 0.8325 to 0.8470, ratios 0.8383 to 0.8474). The claim does not state this uncertainty.

The claim reports only mean training-CV ROC-AUC. Average precision is lower for ratios than for raw, ECE is slightly worse, and only some calibration and threshold metrics improve. Selecting on one metric hides mixed evidence.

'Without feature dilution' is not demonstrated. Feature count rises from 11 to about 32, and importance spreads across many correlated ratios with low top10 stability. No ablation or redundancy analysis was done, and importance is not causal evidence.

No decision-time or production-availability review is included. Generic ratio features need domain review of semantics, denominator behavior, and availability at prediction time before any feature is approved. The recommendation should be framed as a screening hypothesis only.

'About 32 features' obscures that the matrix varies by fold and that the stage definition (cumulative or not, log-denominator ratios included) is not specified. The recipe is not reproducible from this evidence alone.
The selection rule's 0.002 tolerance is below fold-level noise, and six stages were compared on the same 3 folds, so the choice of ratios is within selection-noise range and likely optimistic.

decision: Do not treat EXP-048-C1 as established. At most, retain 'ratios' as one candidate recipe alongside the raw baseline in the next screen, as a screening-stage hypothesis rather than a selected recipe. next_experiment.hypothesis: If the ratios recipe carries real predictive signal beyond raw features, then on identical repeated stratified splits (with duplicate rows kept within one fold side) and with all transformations fit inside each training fold, ratios will show a positive paired ROC-AUC difference over raw that is not driven by a single split. If the EXP-048 gain was fold noise, the paired difference will be indistinguishable from zero.
next_experiment.success_gate: Using 5-fold x 5-repeat CV on the same splits for both recipes, with identical lightgbm params, report the paired mean ROC-AUC difference (ratios minus raw), a 95% interval (paired bootstrap over repeat-fold pairs), and the fraction of pairs where ratios wins. Pass only if the mean difference is >= +0.002, the lower 95% bound is > 0, at least 70% of the 25 pairs favor ratios, and mean log loss and average precision are not worse than raw by more than 0.002. Otherwise the ratios recipe is not supported and raw stays the baseline. A passing result would still be predictive-only evidence and would not approve any feature without decision-time and production-availability review.

risks_and_missing_evidence: Only 3 folds x 1 repeat, so the fold-level variance is very large relative to the 0.0031 gap. The gain is driven by one fold, and ratios is worse than raw in two of three folds.

The 0.002 tolerance in the selection rule is smaller than the fold std of ROC-AUC, so the rule's outcome (ratios vs raw vs interactions) is sensitive to noise. Six stages were compared on the same folds, so the winner is subject to selection optimism (winner's curse).
All evidence is training-CV. No untouched holdout or temporal/grouped validation result is cited. The claim says 'training-CV' but the question asks about validation evidence.

There is no evidence on how the CV splits were built: stratification, duplicate-row handling (wine datasets are known to contain repeated rows, so duplicates across train/validation folds should be checked), or grouping. Overlap would inflate all stages and could favor higher-capacity feature sets.

It is not documented that ratio/log/interaction transformations (including any clipping, zero-denominator handling, and log1p offsets) were fit strictly within each training fold. The 'train-fitted' property is asserted in the question but not evidenced.

Feature matrices differ per fold (fractional feature_count_mean, observed_folds below 3). The recipe is therefore not a fixed feature list, and 'about 32 features' is a mean. It is unclear whether the ratios stage is cumulative (it contains log1p-denominator ratios) or ratios-only.

The 'selected' stage (25 features) scored lowest, and it is not documented whether feature selection was nested inside CV. If it used importances from data including validation folds, it would be leaky. Its poor score does not confirm or rule this out. The stage name also overlaps with the selection_rule, which is ambiguous.
Secondary metrics are mixed: average precision and ECE favor raw, while accuracy, F1, log loss and Brier favor ratios. Accuracy and F1 use a fixed 0.5 threshold with no decision-cost justification.

Feature-importance stability is a model-internal heuristic. It is split across correlated ratios and does not show causal or semantic value. The ratio drop of total_sulfur_dioxide importance is consistent with redundancy, not necessarily dilution.
Default LightGBM params only. The ratio gain may not persist after tuning or on other model families, and the evidence may not generalize beyond lightgbm.

Production semantics are unreviewed: whether the underlying chemistry measurements (for example free vs total sulfur dioxide) are available at the decision time, whether ratio denominators can be zero or noisy in production, and whether the target definition and binarization are appropriate. The claim's own limitation says a domain expert must review this. The bundle-level limitations list is empty.

challenges_to_claims.issue: The claim names 'ratios features' as part of the candidate, but the bundle has no non-ratio stage for comparison, so any benefit of the ratio features is unsupported. Their decision-time and production availability is also unreviewed.

The ±0.0036 is a std over only 3 folds with 1 repeat, and fold splitting (duplicates, grouping, stratification) is undocumented. Duplicate leakage could inflate high-capacity models such as extra_trees.
The ranking compares untuned default configurations ('baseline'), so 'strongest algorithm family' is not established. It reflects only this default-parameter comparison.

The claim is worded as a recommendation and correctly notes the unseen holdout, but the bundle's limitations are empty and leave out the validation risks above. It should not be read as cleared for promotion.

next_experiment.success_gate: On training data only, with identical duplicate-grouped, stratified folds (5 folds × 3 repeats, fixed seeds, feature generation fit inside each training fold), extra_trees beats lightgbm in at least 80% of paired folds with a mean paired ROC-AUC difference ≥ 0.01. Its mean minus 0.25×std score must also remain the highest of the two models. If the paired difference falls below 0.01 or the sign flips in more than 20% of paired folds, the 'extra_trees leader' claim is falsified or downgraded to a tie. Duplicate-row counts and the fold construction are reported either way.
next_experiment.title: Duplicate-aware repeated CV re-check of extra_trees vs lightgbm on the ratios feature set
next_experiment.why_smallest: It re-runs only the top two models, once, on the same feature stage with no tuning and no holdout access. It tests the two biggest threats to the claim (split leakage and small-sample instability) before spending effort on tuning or feature review.

risks_and_missing_evidence: No evidence on duplicate or near-duplicate rows or on grouping. Wine-quality-style data often contains repeated measurement rows, and these can leak across random folds and favour high-capacity, memorising learners like extra_trees. The fold construction (stratified, grouped, seeded) is not documented in the bundle.
3 folds × 1 repeat gives a very small sample for the std and CI. The ±0.0036 is a fold std, not a confidence interval for generalisation.
All models use baseline defaults with no tuning. A family ranking from untuned defaults is confounded with default-hyperparameter fit, especially for the boosters.
Only the 'ratios' stage appears in this evidence. There is no comparison to raw or other feature stages, so it cannot be said that the ratio features help. The candidate is tied to this feature set.

Feature count varies across folds (feature_count_mean 32.33, some features seen in 2 of 3 folds). It is unclear whether feature generation or selection is fitted inside each training fold, which would be needed to rule out preprocessing leakage.

Decision-time and production-availability review is absent for the engineered ratio and log1p features, as well as the raw ones. Wine-quality chemistry features may or may not be available at the real decision time, and the bundle does not say.

The target definition (binarisation rule, class prevalence, red/white mixing) and the fixed 0.5 threshold are not documented. Threshold-dependent metrics (accuracy, F1, precision, recall) are therefore not decision-grade.
Impurity-style importances are unstable across folds. For example, top10_frequency of 0.33–0.67 for many features and model-specific rankings mean they cannot support feature-level or causal claims.
extra_trees has a higher mean ece_10 than logistic_regression, and the calibration gap was not tested. There is no runtime/cost context beyond a sub-3-second elapsed time.
There is no holdout evidence, as the claim's own limitation states, and the bundle's limitations list is empty despite the issues above.

challenges_to_claims.issue: The numeric values are traceable to the cited paths. However, 'preselected' and 'extra_trees/baseline' are not supported by the cited evidence, and the claim carries no limitations (split design, holdout size, duplicate audit, CI scope). Presenting it as unqualified fact overstates certainty.
The claim does not address the experiment's question about the CV gain from optimization, because no CV comparison is cited. Any inference that tuning helped or did not help is unsupported.

The recommendation is reasonable, but the cited stability evidence uses only 3 folds, and importances are correlated and nearly flat after the top feature. No feature has been reviewed for decision-time or production availability, so the evidence cannot support promoting any feature. Importance also must not be read as causal.

decision: Report EXP-050-C1 only as the observed holdout ROC-AUC of the chosen recipe with its bootstrap interval. Make no claim that optimization improved CV performance until the CV candidate comparison is supplied. Do not approve any feature or the model for deployment. EXP-050-C2 is acceptable as a cautionary recommendation, but it is a rule statement, not a feature-level review.

next_experiment.hypothesis: The best tuned candidate does not improve training-CV ROC-AUC over the extra_trees baseline by more than fold noise (a null of ≤0.001 paired mean difference). This is falsified if the paired difference is reliably ≥0.001.
next_experiment.success_gate: Using identical repeated stratified folds (e.g., 5x3) with duplicate rows grouped into the same fold, and feature engineering fit inside each fold, report per-fold ROC-AUC for the baseline and each tuned candidate. The hypothesis is falsified, and the gain is called meaningful, only if the mean paired difference is ≥0.001 AND the 95% interval of paired differences excludes 0. Otherwise report no demonstrated gain. Also report the count of train/holdout duplicate or near-duplicate rows, and add permutation importance with per-fold rank correlation as the stability check.
next_experiment.title: Paired repeated-CV comparison of baseline vs tuned candidates with duplicate-aware folds (no holdout use)
next_experiment.why_smallest: It reuses the existing candidate set and selection rule, needs no new model families and no holdout access, and directly produces the missing CV evidence together with the missing leakage and variance checks.

risks_and_missing_evidence: No CV scores for baseline or tuned candidates are in the bundle (evidence.selection_rule gives only the rule). The 'meaningful CV gain' question is unanswered, and the 0.001 threshold is small relative to likely fold-to-fold variance.

The preselection claim cannot be verified from the evidence: there is no timestamp, config hash or log showing the recipe was fixed before the holdout was scored (evidence.holdout_consumed is only a boolean).
The limitations lists are empty in both claims and the bundle, although holdout size, class prevalence, target definition and split method are not reported.

Possible duplicate or near-duplicate rows across train and holdout are not audited. The wine-quality data is commonly reported to contain many duplicate rows, so this could inflate holdout ROC-AUC. This is a hypothesis to check, not an observed fact.
The bootstrap CI (400 draws) covers holdout sampling variance only, not training-set or seed variance. It also gives no repeated-split estimate.
Metrics at threshold 0.5 are reported with no justification of the threshold and no prevalence baseline, so accuracy, precision and recall are hard to interpret.

It is not shown that engineered features (log1p, ratios) were built inside the CV pipeline. observed_folds of 2 for some features suggests the feature set varies by fold, and the cause is unexplained.

Only 3 CV folds were used for stability, so top10_frequency has coarse resolution (0, 1/3, 2/3, 1). The importance type (impurity vs permutation) is not stated, and impurity importance is biased with correlated and derived features.
No decision-time availability or production-availability review is documented for any feature, and no monitoring plan is given. The package states the rule but does not apply it.
Because the holdout is consumed, any further tuning or model selection on it would be contaminated.
